draft.title: Learning from a mentor text
card: A mentor text is a short published piece that you read closely to learn how the writer worked. You read it as a writer, not only as a reader.
Choose one technique to study, such as the opening move, the structure or a recurring image. Ask what the writer did and why it works.
Borrow the technique, not the words. Use the same move in your own piece, with your own subject, ideas and sentences.
Copying a writer's sentences or ideas is plagiarism. Learning how a writer built a piece, then building your own, is not.
draft.remember: Study how a mentor text works, then use that technique in your own words.

a.q: What is the best way to use a mentor text in your own writing?
opts: Borrow one technique and apply it to your own subject
Copy its best sentences and change a few words
Write about the same topic using the same ideas
Read it once for enjoyment and then put it aside
a.why: A mentor text teaches a technique you can reuse with your own content. Copying sentences or ideas is plagiarism, and reading only for enjoyment skips the close study that makes it useful.
a.clue: You take the method, not the writer's content.

b.q: Priya reads a short article that begins with a startling one-line sentence. She starts her own story about a school camp with a startling one-line sentence of her own. What has she done?
opts: Borrowed the opening technique and used it in her own piece
Copied the article's opening and changed the topic
Plagiarised the article by using a similar sentence length
Studied the article's structure without using any technique
b.why: Priya has borrowed a technique, a striking short opening, and used it with her own subject and words. This is not copying, because she has not taken the article's sentence or ideas. A similar move is not plagiarism.
b.clue: Did she take the writer's words, or only the writer's method?

a.best: Borrow one technique and apply it to your own subject

b.best: Borrowed the opening technique and used it in her own piece
